summary: This unit teaches you to use a smartphone or tablet safely and well at work. You will learn to operate, charge and care for the device, connect it to networks, use its apps to record and share your work, keep the device and its information secure, respect other people's privacy, and sort out common problems.

blocks.p: Smartphones and tablets are now work tools. A welder sends photos of a finished gate to the supervisor, an electrician looks up a wiring diagram and books the next visit in the calendar, and a villa attendant records room checks on a tablet and messages the manager about a leaking tap. This unit teaches you to use a **mobile IT device** in ways that are safe, secure, polite and useful to your employer.

**Who it is for:** this is a general unit in several Level 2 programmes, including Welding and Hospitality (villa and property services), so the examples come from workshops, building sites, homes and villas. It suits anyone who uses a phone or tablet for work, whether it belongs to the employer or to you.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Know the device
Name the main types of mobile device and their parts, and say what each part does.
Operate it
Switch on, unlock, use the touch screen and settings, open and close apps, and take screenshots.
Charge and care for it
Charge it safely, look after the battery, protect it from heat, water, dust and knocks, and clean it correctly.
Connect it
Use Wi-Fi, mobile data, Bluetooth, a hotspot and airplane mode, and know the risks of public Wi-Fi.
Use apps for work
Install apps safely, check permissions and updates, and use the camera, calendar, maps, notes, calculator, email and messages.
Record and share evidence
Take clear photos and notes of work, label them, and send them to the right person through the agreed channel.
Keep it secure
Use a screen lock, strong passwords and two-step verification, spot scams, back up, and act fast if the device is lost.
Respect privacy and use it safely
Ask before photographing people, protect customers' and guests' information, and never use the device where it is unsafe.
Solve common problems
Fix simple faults (no Wi-Fi, a frozen app, full storage) and report the ones you cannot fix.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on device parts, touch-screen use, charging and care, connections, apps, photos as evidence, security, scams, privacy, safe use and simple fault-finding.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as icon, screenshot, QR code, GPS, PIN, malware, SIM card, sync) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: recording, labelling and sending job evidence with a device; and setting up, securing and fixing faults on a training device. You must never show a password or PIN in a screenshot.

blocks.note: Your employer's rules on phones come first. Some workplaces ban personal phones in certain areas, or give staff a work phone or tablet with its own rules. Ask before you use your own phone for work.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Mobile devices and how to operate them

head: Device
What it is
Work examples
rows: Smartphone
A phone that is also a small computer, with a touch screen, camera, internet and apps
Calls and messages to the supervisor; photos of finished work; maps to a new site
Tablet
A larger touch-screen device, often with Wi-Fi only, sometimes with a SIM card
Room checklists in a villa; drawings and manuals on site; showing customers photos of past jobs
Laptop
A portable computer with a keyboard, run from a battery
Typing reports and quotations on site
Wearable
A smartwatch or fitness band linked to a phone
Seeing who is calling without taking the phone out
Handheld work device
A device made for one job, such as a card payment machine or a stock scanner
Taking payment at a counter; checking stock in a store room

blocks.h: The parts of a smartphone or tablet

head: Part
What it does
rows: Touch screen
Shows everything and takes your taps and swipes
Power (side) button
Turns the device on and off and locks the screen
Volume buttons
Change the sound level; often used with the power button for a screenshot
Cameras and flash
Take photos and videos; the flash can also be used as a torch
Microphone and speaker
For calls, voice notes and video
Charging port
Where the charging cable plugs in; some devices also charge on a wireless pad
SIM card (or eSIM)
The small card from the phone network, or a built-in digital version, that holds your number and lets the device use the network
Battery
Built in, and almost always **lithium-ion**: light and powerful, but easily damaged by heat and knocks
Storage
Where apps, photos and files are kept, measured in gigabytes (GB); some devices also take a memory card
Sensors
GPS for location, a fingerprint reader or face camera for unlocking, and others

ul: Press the power button to wake the device, then unlock it with your PIN, pattern, password, fingerprint or face.
The **home screen** holds the **icons** (small pictures) that open the **apps**. App is short for **application**: a program on the device.

**Notifications** (new messages, missed calls, reminders) appear at the top of the screen. Swipe down to see them and to reach quick settings such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, airplane mode, the torch and screen brightness.
The **Settings** app holds every setting: Wi-Fi, display, sound, security, storage, battery, accessibility and updates.
Back, home and recent-apps controls take you back a step, to the home screen, or to a list of open apps. On some devices they are buttons; on others they are swipes from the bottom edge.

head: Touch action
How you do it
What it usually does
rows: Tap
Touch the screen once, briefly
Opens an app or picks an item
Double-tap
Tap twice quickly
Zooms in on a photo or page
Long press
Press and hold one spot
Shows more options, such as copy, or lets you move an icon
Swipe
Slide a finger across the screen
Moves between pages or photos; opens menus
Drag
Press, hold and slide
Moves an item to a new place
Spread
Move two fingers apart on the screen
Zooms in
Pinch
Move two fingers together
Zooms out

ul: The on-screen keyboard has **autocorrect**, which can change a word into the wrong one. Read every work message before you send it. Voice typing turns speech into text, but check it too.
To copy text, long-press a word, drag the handles to select, then choose Copy; long-press where it is to go and choose Paste.

A **screenshot** saves a picture of exactly what is on the screen. On many devices you press the power button and a volume button together; check the method for yours. Never screenshot a password, PIN or a customer's private details.

A **QR code** is a square black-and-white pattern. Point the camera at it to open a link, a Wi-Fi log-in or a menu. Look at the web address the phone shows before you open it: criminals sometimes stick a fake QR code over a real one.

blocks.h: Making the device easier to use

blocks.p: **Accessibility** settings help everyone: bigger text, display zoom, a magnifier that uses the camera, read-aloud, captions, and dark mode. A person with poor eyesight, or anyone working in bright sun, may find these make the device far easier to read.

head: Unit
About how much
Example
rows: Kilobyte (KB)
1,000 bytes
A short text file
Megabyte (MB)
One phone photo is often 2 to 5 MB
Gigabyte (GB)
A 64 GB phone holds many thousands of photos, but far less video
Terabyte (TB)
Computer drives and large cloud accounts

blocks.note: Video takes far more space than photos: a minute of high-quality video can be well over 100 MB. When storage runs out, videos are usually the first place to look.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Charging, battery care and protecting the device

blocks.p: The **lithium-ion battery** inside a phone or tablet stores a lot of energy in a small space. Treated well, it lasts for years. Damaged, overheated or charged with poor equipment, it can swell, catch fire or even burst.

ul: Use the maker's charger or a good-quality one made for your device, with a cable that is not split, kinked or burnt.
Charge on a hard surface where air can reach the device: a desk or shelf, never under a pillow, on a bed or under clothes.
Do not charge in direct sun, near a stove or heater, or near water, and never charge a device that is wet.
Unplug the charger from the wall when you have finished. In a thunderstorm, unplug chargers or use a surge protector.
Keep a charged **power bank** (a portable battery) for long days on site and for power cuts.

blocks.note: If a device gets very hot, smells of burning, hisses, or its back or screen bulges because the battery has **swollen**, stop using and charging it at once. Unplug it, put it on a hard surface away from anything that burns, do not press or pierce it, and report it. Never throw a damaged battery or device in the household rubbish or a fire: hand it in for proper disposal.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Heat is a battery's worst enemy. Keep the device out of the sun and never leave it on a car dashboard or seat in a parked vehicle.
Many batteries last longest if they are not left at 100% for long or run right down to 0% often. Charging little and often is fine.
Battery saver mode, a dimmer screen, and turning off Bluetooth, location and apps you are not using all make a charge last longer.
A weak signal drains the battery fast, because the phone keeps searching. In a basement or the hills, airplane mode with Wi-Fi on can help.

blocks.note: Jamaica's sun can make a parked vehicle's dashboard hot enough to burn your hand, and that is enough to damage a battery and screen. Keep the device in your pocket, a bag in the shade or a locker. Phones also overheat if they are used hard (video, maps, games) while charging in a hot room.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Danger
How to protect the device
rows: Drops and knocks
A strong case and a screen protector; a lanyard or belt holster on site; never in a back pocket when you bend or climb
Water
Keep it out of bathrooms, kitchens, sinks, pools and the rain. A "water-resistant" device is not waterproof, its seals wear with age, and water damage is often not covered by the warranty.
Dust, sparks and spatter
Keep it out of welding and grinding areas, in a pocket or locker. Sparks and spatter pit the screen and lens; grinding dust gets into ports and buttons.
Chemicals
Keep it away from bleach, oven cleaner, solvents and pool chemicals, which damage the screen coating and case
Sand and heat on the beach or by the pool
Keep it in a bag in the shade; sand scratches the screen and blocks the ports

flow: Switch the device off and unplug it
Wipe the screen and case with a soft, lint-free cloth (such as microfibre)
If it is still dirty, use the cloth slightly damp with water, or a wipe the maker says is safe
Never spray liquid straight onto it, soak it, or use bleach, scouring pads or rough paper
Clear a dusty port gently with a soft, dry brush, never with a pin or metal point

head: Connection
What it is
Use it for
Watch out for
rows: Wi-Fi
A wireless link to a local network and the internet through a router
Large files, many photos, video calls and updates, where there is a trusted network
Public and unknown networks; the password is case-sensitive
Mobile data
Internet through the phone network, using your SIM
Messages, email, maps and small files where there is no Wi-Fi
It uses up your data plan; the signal is weak in some hills and buildings
Bluetooth
A short-range wireless link between devices close together
Earpieces and hands-free sets, speakers, small printers, a smartwatch
Pair only with devices you know; turn it off when not needed
Hotspot
Your phone shares its mobile data with other devices by Wi-Fi
Letting a laptop send a file when there is no other internet
It uses your data fast; always set a password on it
Airplane (aeroplane or flight) mode
Turns off the phone's wireless signals in one tap
Flights; saving battery where there is no signal. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth can be switched back on while it is on.
You cannot get calls or texts while it is on
Location (GPS)
Works out where the device is, using satellites and nearby signals
Maps and directions; sharing where you are; finding a lost device
Photos may record where they were taken; apps may track you
NFC
A very short-range link, used by holding devices close together
Tap-to-pay and some door cards
Keep payment features locked behind the screen lock

flow: Open Settings (or quick settings) and switch Wi-Fi on
Check that airplane mode is off, or that Wi-Fi is on within it
Pick the right network name; ask staff for the exact name if you are not sure
Type the password exactly: capitals and small letters count
Check that it says Connected, then open a web page to test it

ul: Many people in Jamaica buy data plans or top up prepaid credit, so data costs money. Check your data use in Settings.
Send large files and many photos, and install updates, on a trusted Wi-Fi network.
Turn off auto-play of videos and automatic download of media in chat apps if your data runs out quickly.

blocks.p: Free Wi-Fi in a plaza, a café, a hotel lobby or an airport is handy but not private. Other people on it, or a criminal who sets up a fake network with a similar name, may be able to see or steal what you send.

ul: Do not log in to work accounts, banking or email on public Wi-Fi. Use your mobile data instead.
Check the network's exact name with the staff before you join.
Turn off automatic joining of open networks, and tell the device to forget a public network when you leave.
Never share your own hotspot password with strangers.

Install apps only from the device's **official app store** (or the store your employer's IT department uses). Apps from links in messages, unknown websites or memory cards can carry **malware**: harmful software that damages a device or steals its data.
Before installing, check the maker's name, the reviews and the number of downloads. A fake app often copies a real one's name with a small change.
Free apps may be paid for by adverts or by collecting your data. Watch for in-app purchases.
Delete apps you no longer use: they take space, may run in the background, and still hold your data.

blocks.p: When an app asks for **permission** to use the camera, microphone, location, contacts, photos or messages, ask: does it need this to do its job? A camera app needs the camera; a calculator does not need your contacts. Refuse what is not needed, and choose "only while using the app" for location where you can. You can change permissions later in Settings.

System and app **updates** fix faults and close security holes that criminals use. Install them when they are offered, on Wi-Fi, with the battery well charged or the device on charge. Restart the device afterwards if it asks.

head: App
How it helps at work
rows: Camera and gallery (photos)
Evidence of finished work, faults, damage and stock; showing customers past jobs
Notes
Measurements, materials lists, guest requests, serial numbers
Calendar
Job times, site visits, guest arrivals, with reminders and the customer's details in the event
Maps (GPS)
Directions to a new site or villa; sharing a location pin; offline maps for areas with poor signal
Calculator
Quick sums: lengths, areas, quantities, costs
Clock
Alarms, timers (for example paint drying or a cleaning product's contact time) and a stopwatch
Email
Reports, quotations, job photos and attachments to supervisors and customers
Messages and chat apps
Quick updates to the supervisor and team, in the work group the employer sets up
Voice recorder
A quick spoken note when your hands are dirty (never record people without their permission)
Document scanner
Turns a photo of a signed job card or receipt into a neat PDF
Cloud storage
Keeps work files and photos safe off the device and shares them with the team
Torch
Light for looking under sinks, inside panels or into dark corners
Translation
Helps with a guest or customer who speaks another language

blocks.p: A good calendar event can be acted on by anyone who reads it. Give it a clear title, the date and start time, the place (with a location pin if you have one), the customer's name and phone number, what the job is, and a reminder far enough ahead to get there.

blocks.note: Many rural Jamaican addresses are a district and a landmark ("past the church, the green gate after the shop") rather than a street and number. Ask the customer to send a **location pin** from their phone, save it in the calendar event, and download the area's map for offline use before you drive into hills with poor signal.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep work messages short, clear and polite: who, what, where, when. Use proper words, not text slang, and no ALL CAPITALS.
Email needs a clear subject line, a greeting, the message, and your name and job title at the end. Attach files, then check they are attached.
Check who you are sending to before you press Send, especially in group chats.
Answer work messages in working hours unless it is urgent, and use the channel your employer has agreed.

sections.title: Recording and sharing evidence of work

blocks.p: Photos, short videos and notes from a mobile device are now normal evidence of work: a finished weld, a fitted gate, a tested circuit, a room made ready for guests, or damage found before you started. Good evidence protects you, your employer and the customer.

flow: Check that photos are allowed here, and that no people or private items will be in them
Make sure you are safe: standing still, on the ground, away from hot work, water and traffic
Clean the lens; get good light (use the flash or torch in dark places)
Take a wide photo to show where the work is, then close-ups to show the detail
Put a tape measure or rule in the photo where size matters
Check each photo is sharp; take another if not
Label it: job, place, date and what it shows
Send it to the right person through the agreed app or email, with a short message
File it in the work folder and delete personal copies when the job is closed, as your workplace's rules say

head: Good evidence photo
Poor evidence photo
rows: Sharp, well lit, taken square on
Blurred, dark, or taken at a sharp angle
A wide shot and close-ups
One close-up that does not show where it is
A rule or tape in the shot for size
No way of judging size
Before, during and after, when asked
Only the finished job, so problems found earlier cannot be shown
Labelled with job, place and date
An unlabelled photo among hundreds in the gallery
Only the work, nothing private
A guest's belongings, a family photo or an alarm code in the background

ul: Phones record the **date and time** in each photo's details, and often the location too. This helps prove when work was done. Turn off location in photos you may share publicly.

Many chat apps **shrink photos** to send them faster, and fine detail (a model number, a hairline crack) can be lost. When detail matters, send the original file by email or through the work cloud folder.
Keep each job's photos in an album or folder named for the job, so they are easy to find and send.
A short video can show a fault that a photo cannot, such as a gate that sticks or a light that flickers. Keep it short: video files are large.
Write measurements and readings in the notes app straight away, with units (mm, m, A, V) and the place.
Scan a signed job card or delivery note with a document scanner app and send it as a PDF.
Use a voice note only when typing is not practical, and keep it short and clear.

sections.title: Keeping the device and its information secure

blocks.p: A work device may hold customers' names, addresses and phone numbers, guests' details, job photos, prices and the log-ins to work accounts. If it falls into the wrong hands, all of that is exposed. Protect it in layers.

head: Protection
What to do
rows: Screen lock
Use a PIN (personal identification number), pattern, password, fingerprint or face. Set it to lock itself after a short time, such as 30 seconds to 1 minute. Hide message content on the lock screen.
Passwords
Long and hard to guess: a passphrase of several words with numbers and symbols is good. Use a different one for every account. Never share it or write it where others see it.
Two-step verification
Turn it on for email and work accounts, so a code (by text or from an app) is needed as well as the password.
One-time codes
A code sent to your phone is for you alone. No real bank, phone company or employer will ever ask you to read it out.
Updates
Install system and app updates promptly.
Apps
Only from the official store, with only the permissions they need.
Backup and sync
Turn on automatic backup to cloud storage or a computer, and check that it runs. Sync keeps contacts, calendar and files the same on all your devices.
Find my device
Turn on the setting that lets a lost device be located, made to ring, locked or erased from another device.

head: Scam
What it looks like
What to do
rows: Phishing (by email) and smishing (by text)
A message that looks like it is from a bank, delivery service, phone company or employer, with a link or attachment and a reason to hurry
Do not click or reply. Check by contacting the company on a number you know is real.
Vishing (by phone call)
A caller who claims to be from your bank or the phone company and asks for codes, PINs or card details
Hang up. Call the company back on the number on your card or their official website.
Prize and lottery scams
"You have won!" for a draw you never entered, with a fee to pay first
Never pay to collect a prize. Delete and report it.
SIM swap
A criminal tricks the phone company into moving your number to their SIM, so they get your codes. Your phone suddenly shows "No service" for a long time.
Contact your phone company at once, from another phone if you have to.
Fake apps and links
An app or link that copies a real one, asking you to log in
Use only the official store and type web addresses yourself.

blocks.note: Jamaica has a long-running problem with lottery scam calls and messages, and fake "parcel fee" and "account blocked" texts are common everywhere. Real organisations do not demand payment through a link in a text, and never ask for your one-time code. If you clicked or gave details, tell your supervisor and call your bank straight away: speed limits the damage.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Pop-ups that will not go away, apps you did not install, the battery draining much faster than usual, the device getting hot when idle, or data being used up quickly can all be signs of **malware**. Do not try fixes from strangers online: report it to your supervisor or IT support.

blocks.h: If a work device is lost or stolen

flow: Report it to your supervisor at once: it may hold customers', guests' and business information
From another device, use find my device to see where it is, make it ring, or lock it with a message
Erase it remotely only as the last resort, when it cannot be recovered: once erased, many devices can no longer be located
Change the passwords of the email, cloud and work accounts that were on it
If it was stolen, report it to the police, and ask the phone company to block the SIM (they can give you a new SIM with the same number)

blocks.note: Every phone has a unique **IMEI** number, which the police and phone company use to identify it. Find it in Settings (About phone), on the box, or by dialling *#06#, and keep a note of it somewhere other than the phone.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Using the device safely, politely and privately

head: Situation
Why not
What to do instead
rows: Driving
Reading or typing takes your eyes and mind off the road. Jamaica's road traffic law does not allow a driver to hold and use a phone while driving.
Pull over safely first, or use a hands-free set only where the law allows
On a ladder, roof or scaffold
You need both hands and your full attention to stay safe
Let calls go to voicemail; call back from the ground
Running a grinder, welding or using power tools
A moment's distraction can cause a serious injury
Stop the machine and make it safe before you look
Walking through a workshop or site
You can trip on cables, walk into a hazard or into a work area without PPE
Stop and stand somewhere safe to use it
Near hot work, water or chemicals
Sparks, spatter, splashes and steam damage the device
Leave it in a pocket, bag or locker away from the work
With a guest or customer, or in a meeting
It looks rude and careless, and they feel ignored
Put it on silent or vibrate; take personal calls on your break

blocks.note: Earphones in both ears on site or near traffic stop you hearing shouted warnings, reversing alarms and machines. Keep the volume low, or use one earpiece only where your workplace allows it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Hold the device up nearer eye level instead of bending your neck down for long periods.
Rest your eyes and thumbs: short breaks, and look into the distance now and again.
Turn the brightness down indoors and at night, and use larger text if you are squinting.

blocks.h: Privacy of customers, guests and co-workers

ul: Photograph only what the job needs. **Ask permission** before any person is in a photo or video, and never record a conversation without permission.

In a customer's home or a guest's villa, keep private things out of your pictures: documents, money, jewellery, family photos, children, and security features such as alarm panels, safes, keys and gate codes. Do not move guests' belongings to get a better shot.
Never post work photos, addresses or guest details on your personal social media, or share them in personal chat groups.
Send work information only to people who need it, through the work channel, and keep the device locked so others cannot see it.
Delete work photos from your own phone when the job is closed, if your workplace's rules say so.

Jamaica's data protection law expects businesses to keep personal information about customers and guests safe and use it only for the reason it was collected. As a worker, you help by following these rules.

blocks.p: Most employers have rules on mobile devices: where phones may be used, which apps and groups are used for work, whether you may use your own phone (and what must be on it if you do), photos, and what to do if a device is lost. Following them keeps work **safe, private and professional**, and protects you if something goes wrong.

Many faults are fixed by a simple check or a restart. Work through the checks in order, write down what you tried, and report what you cannot fix. Do not reset a work device to factory settings, take it apart, or install "fixing" apps from strangers: that can lose data and break the employer's settings.

head: Problem
Check first
Then
rows: Will not connect to Wi-Fi
Wi-Fi is on and airplane mode is off
The right network is chosen and the password is typed exactly
Move closer to the router; turn Wi-Fi off and on; restart the device
If other devices cannot connect either, report the network fault
No mobile data
Mobile data is switched on
There is a signal, and data or credit left on the plan
Toggle airplane mode on and off; restart
Long "No service" when others have signal: contact the phone company
An app freezes or keeps closing
Close the app fully and open it again
Restart the device; check for app and system updates; report if it keeps happening
The whole device is frozen
Wait a minute in case it is busy
Force a restart with the button method the maker gives for your model
Storage full
See what uses the most space in Settings (Storage)
Check the backup has finished, then delete videos and photos already backed up, apps you do not use and old downloads
Battery drains fast
Screen brightness, location, Bluetooth and apps running in the background
Use battery saver; close unused apps; report a battery that is old, hot or swollen
Will not charge
Try another socket and a cable you know works; look for dust in the port
Clean the port gently with a soft dry brush; report it if it still will not charge
Too hot
Is it in the sun, in a case, charging, or running video or maps?
Stop using it, take it out of the case and let it cool in the shade. Never put it in a fridge.
No sound on calls or alerts
Volume, silent switch, and do-not-disturb
Check that Bluetooth is not sending the sound to an earpiece
Will not pair with an earpiece
Bluetooth is on and the earpiece is charged and in pairing mode
Remove (forget) the old pairing and pair again

flow: Take it out of the water and switch it off
Do not charge it or plug anything in
Wipe it dry, remove the case, and gently tap it with the charging port facing down
Leave it to dry in a dry place with moving air; do not use a hair dryer, an oven or other heat
Report it if it is a work device, and do not switch it on until it is fully dry

blocks.note: Putting a wet phone in a bag of rice is a popular idea, but some phone makers advise against it: rice does not dry the inside faster than air, and its dust can get into the ports.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it on a device with your instructor.

ul: I can name the main types of mobile IT device and the parts of a smartphone or tablet.
I can use the touch screen: tap, double-tap, long press, swipe, drag, spread and pinch.
I can find and change settings, take a screenshot and scan a QR code safely.
I can charge a device safely, care for its battery, and say what to do if a battery swells or overheats.
I can protect a device from heat, water, dust, sparks and knocks, and clean it correctly.
I can explain Wi-Fi, mobile data, Bluetooth, a hotspot, airplane mode and GPS, and say when to use each.
I can explain the risks of public Wi-Fi.
I can install apps safely, check their permissions and keep them updated.
I can use the camera, notes, calendar, maps, calculator, email and messages for work.
I can take, label and send clear photos as evidence of work.
I can set a screen lock, use strong passwords and two-step verification, and keep one-time codes private.
I can recognise phishing, smishing, vishing, prize scams and a SIM swap, and say what to do.
I can back up a device and say what to do if it is lost or stolen.
I can respect the privacy of customers, guests and co-workers.
I can say when and where not to use a device, and why.
I can fix simple faults and report the ones I cannot fix.

terms: A setting that turns off the device's wireless signals; also called aeroplane or flight mode
A program on a phone, tablet or computer
A copy of files and settings kept somewhere else, so they can be restored
A short-range wireless link between devices close together
Storing files on the internet so they can be reached from any device
A unit of storage: about 1,000 megabytes
Global positioning system: works out where the device is
The main screen after unlocking, with the app icons
A phone sharing its mobile data with other devices by Wi-Fi
A small picture you tap to open an app
The unique number that identifies a mobile phone
The rechargeable battery in most phones and tablets
Harmful software that can damage a device or steal its data
Internet through the phone network, using the SIM
An alert on the screen about a message, call or reminder
Access an app asks for, such as to the camera, location or contacts
A fake message that tries to trick you into giving passwords or bank details; smishing by text, vishing by phone call
A portable battery for charging a device away from a socket
A square pattern scanned with the camera to open a link
A PIN, pattern, password, fingerprint or face check that stops others using the device
A saved picture of exactly what is on the screen
The card from the phone network that holds your number and lets the device use the network
A fraud in which a criminal moves your phone number to their SIM
Keeping the same files, contacts or calendar up to date on two or more devices
A log-in that needs a code as well as the password
A new version of the system or an app that fixes faults and security holes
A wireless link to a local network and the internet

c1.title: Room checks at a villa in Negril
c1.text: Tamara is an attendant at a villa in Negril, Westmoreland. She uses the villa company's tablet to record room checks and send photos to her supervisor. Today she has found a leaking tap under a bathroom sink in the garden cottage. The tablet's storage is 95% full and its backup ran last night. The villa's Wi-Fi reaches only the main house; in the cottage the mobile signal is weak. She has taken 20 photos of the cottage rooms and the tap.

c2.title: Outside lights on a roof in Portmore
c2.text: Rohan is an electrician's helper fixing outside lights on a house roof in Portmore, St Catherine. He left his phone on the van dashboard all morning in the sun. At lunch it shows a temperature warning and will not charge. He has been charging it with a cheap cable whose outer cover is split near the plug. In the afternoon, while he is up the ladder, the phone rings.

c3.title: A farm gate near Frankfield
c3.text: Garfield, a welder, must repair a farm gate in a hill district near Frankfield, Clarendon. There is no street name or number: the farmer says, "Pass the church, then it's the green gate after the shop." The mobile signal is patchy in the hills. After the repair, the gate must be checked again and painted in two weeks.

c4.title: A lost tablet in Falmouth
c4.text: Nickeisha works for a contractor building a hotel extension in Falmouth, Trelawny. The company tablet she uses for site photos, notes and the client's contact list has gone missing from the site office. It has a screen lock, and find my device is turned on. Its backup is set to run on Wi-Fi only, and it last ran three days ago.

c5.title: A text message at a guest house in Christiana
c5.text: Kerene works at the front desk of a guest house in Christiana, Manchester. The work phone gets a text: "Your parcel is held at customs. Pay J$1,500 fee within 2 hours or it will be returned: " followed by a link. Kerene is expecting linen from a supplier, so she clicks the link and types in the guest house's card details before she feels something is wrong. The next morning, the work phone shows "No service" for hours, while everyone else's phone has a signal.

questions.q: To free space on the tablet quickly, which files should Tamara look at first?
o: Contacts saved in the address book
Text messages from the last few months
Old videos already backed up
Calendar entries for all the past jobs
questions.why: Video takes far more space than anything else: a minute can be over 100 MB. Delete only what the backup already holds, and check with the supervisor if the files are work evidence.

questions.q: What is the best way to get the 20 photos to her supervisor?
o: Message now, then send the photos on the main house Wi-Fi
Keep trying to send all 20 over the weak signal until they go
Wait and show the supervisor the photos on the tablet next week
Delete half of the photos so that the rest of them send faster
questions.why: Many photos are a large upload, best sent on Wi-Fi. A short message now tells the supervisor about the leak at once, so nothing waits on the photos.

questions.q: The supervisor says the tap's model number cannot be read in the photo sent through the chat app, though it looked sharp on the tablet. What should Tamara do?
o: Send the same photo again through the same chat app
Send the original file by email or the cloud folder
Take a screenshot of the photo and send the screenshot
Turn up the tablet's screen brightness and resend it
questions.why: Many chat apps shrink photos before sending, which loses fine detail. The original file, sent by email or a shared folder, keeps the full detail.

questions.q: Which label should Tamara give the photo of the leaking tap?
o: Look at this, it has been leaking all morning, please call!!
IMG_4471, taken by Tamara on the work tablet this morning
Bathroom photo 3 of 20 from today, please see attached
Leaking tap, cottage bathroom, villa name, date
questions.why: A good label says what the photo shows, where it was taken and when, so anyone can act on it later. A file number or an exclamation tells the reader nothing about the job.

questions.q: What should Rohan do about the hot phone?
o: Put it in the van's cooler box with the ice to cool it fast
Keep it on charge so the battery can recover from the heat
Move it into the shade and let it cool before charging it
Wrap it in a damp cloth and leave it on the bonnet to cool
questions.why: Let an overheated phone cool slowly in the shade. Sudden cold or a damp cloth can let moisture form inside it, and charging adds even more heat.

questions.q: The phone rings while Rohan is up the ladder. What should he do?
o: Answer it quickly, holding the ladder with one hand
Let it ring, and call back once he is on the ground
Wedge the phone between his ear and his shoulder
Answer on speaker and keep the phone in his pocket
questions.why: Work at height needs both hands and full attention. A missed call can be returned in two minutes; a fall cannot be undone.

questions.q: What should he do about the split charging cable?
o: Wrap insulating tape tightly round the split
Use it only during the day when he can see it
Bend the cable so that the split closes up
Stop using it and get a suitable one
questions.why: A damaged cable can short-circuit, overheat or shock, and can harm the battery. Replace it with a charger and cable made for the device; do not patch it.

questions.q: What is the most reliable way for Garfield to find the farm?
o: Ask the farmer to send a location pin
Search the map app for the name of the district
Drive to the church and ask people on the road
Use the phone's compass and head roughly north
questions.why: A location pin is the exact spot, which the map app can then give directions to. It works even where there is no street name, and it can be saved with the job.

questions.q: What should he do before he drives into the hills with patchy signal?
o: Turn on airplane mode so the battery lasts longer on the drive
Download the area's map for offline use while he has signal
Turn off location services so the phone does not search
Delete his other apps so the map app runs faster
questions.why: Many map apps can save an area for offline use, so directions still work when the signal drops. Switching off location would stop the map following him, and airplane mode would stop the farmer reaching him.

questions.q: What should Garfield's calendar entry for the return visit include?
o: Only the word "farm" and the date, to keep it short
The farmer's name, so he can look up the rest later
Date, time, pin, the farmer's number and the job
A photo of the gate, with no date or time added to it
questions.why: A complete entry lets Garfield, or anyone sent in his place, find the place, call the customer and know the job. Add a reminder far enough ahead to plan the trip.

questions.q: After the loss is reported, what can be done from another device with find my device?
o: See where it is, make it ring, lock it or erase it
Switch the tablet on and back up its new photos
Turn the tablet's location off to protect the data
Cancel the tablet's SIM and order a replacement
questions.why: Find my device can locate, ring, lock and, as a last resort, erase the device. Blocking a SIM is done by the phone company, not by this feature.

questions.q: If the tablet is never found, which work is most likely to be lost for good?
o: The client's contact list, saved months ago
Photos and notes from the last three days
Every photo, note and contact on the tablet
Nothing at all, since the tablet has a screen lock
questions.why: Anything backed up three days ago is safe in the backup. Work done since the last backup is only on the tablet. This is why backups should run often and be checked.

questions.q: Why should they try to locate and lock the tablet before erasing it?
o: Erasing it uses up a large amount of data
Erasing it sends all of the photos to the police
Erasing it makes the screen lock stop working
After erasing, many devices cannot be found
questions.why: Erasing wipes the data and, on many devices, stops it being tracked. It is the last step, when the device cannot be got back and its data must be protected.

questions.q: The tablet was logged in to the company email and cloud storage. What else should be done?
o: Delete the company email account for good
Tell the client to change his phone number
Change the passwords for those accounts
Nothing, because the screen lock protects it
questions.why: A screen lock can sometimes be got round, and the accounts may stay logged in. New passwords stop anyone using the lost tablet to reach company email and files.

questions.q: Which part of the text was the strongest sign of a scam?
o: It came while Kerene was at work on a busy weekday
It mentioned a parcel at a time she expected linen
It was written in short and simple English words
It demanded a fee through a link, with a deadline
questions.why: Fake delivery texts rely on an unexpected fee, a link and a short deadline to rush you. A real courier or customs office gives you a reference you can check through its official contact details.

questions.q: Kerene has typed the card details into the page. What should she do first?
o: Wait to see whether any money is taken from the account first
Reply to the text and ask the sender to cancel the payment
Call the bank on the card's number, and tell her supervisor
Delete the message so that nobody else clicks on the link
questions.why: The bank can block the card before the criminals use it, so speed matters. Use the number on the card or the bank's official website, never one in the message.

questions.q: Why should the guest house contact the phone company at once about the "No service" message?
o: The phone's battery may be about to swell
The number may have been moved to a criminal's SIM
The phone may need a software update tonight
The phone company may have cut it off for late payment
questions.why: A long "No service" while others have signal, soon after a scam, can mean a SIM swap: the criminal now gets the calls and one-time codes. The phone company can stop it and restore the number.

questions.q: Which screen-lock setting best protects a work phone that is often left on a counter?
o: Lock after 30 minutes, so it is easy to use
Lock only when the power button is pressed
No lock, so anyone on shift can answer it
Lock after 30 seconds to 1 minute
questions.why: A short auto-lock time means a phone left for a moment is soon locked. A phone that stays open for half an hour gives anyone time to read or send messages.

questions.q: The police ask for the number that identifies a stolen phone. Which number do they mean, and how can you find it?
o: The IMEI; dial *#06# or look in Settings
The PIN; it is shown on the lock screen
The SIM number; it is printed on the charger
The Wi-Fi password; it is on the router
questions.why: Every phone has a unique IMEI, used to identify and block it. Note it down while you have the phone, as you cannot dial *#06# once it is stolen.

questions.q: A villa tablet slips into the pool and is pulled out at once. What should be done?
o: Switch it on to check that it still works
Charge it so the battery does not go flat
Switch it off, wipe it and let it air-dry
Dry it in the oven on a low setting
questions.why: Power and charging can short-circuit a wet device. Switch it off, wipe it, and let it dry in moving air; heat can damage the battery and screen. Report it, as it is a work device.
